paper.title: Valid Best-Model Identification for LLM Evaluation via Low-Rank Factorization

settings.name_in_paper: Best-model identification over a finite benchmark with a budget of T LLM calls (finite-population, sampling without replacement)
unmapped: Each arm's rewards are a finite population of n binary scores (row of score matrix S) sampled uniformly WITHOUT replacement, so observations are not i.i.d.; arm mean is the finite-population mean
Learner has access to predicted scores from a low-rank factorization fitted on side-information score matrix of other models and on observed entries
Learner knows the dataset size n
settings.definition_quote: We let $\mathcal{X} = \{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ be a fixed dataset of examples, $\mathcal{M} = \{f_1,\ldots,f_m\}$ be a set of LLMs. ... $\mu_i = \mathbb{E}[S_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j =1}^{n}S_{i,j}$ ... Given a budget of \(T\) LLM calls ... Our goal is to maximize the probability of correctly identifying the best model \(i^* = \arg\max_{i\in[m]} \mu_i\), which we assume is unique.

symbols.k_pull: pull count K of an arm (summation index)
symbols.a_exp: exploration parameter a of the UCB-E-style index
symbols.v_var: uniform upper bound v on the average conditional variance of the residual correction Z_i
symbols.n_ex: number of examples in the benchmark (n)

conditions: the constant v of Theorem 1 can be chosen uniformly over all models and all pull counts K <= T
pi, lambda and predicted scores are F_{t-1}-measurable (satisfied by construction)

source.label: thm:bandits
source.quote: Let $i^*=\arg\max_{i\in[m]}\mu_i$ be the unique best model, ... Suppose the exploration parameter $a$ satisfies $0\le a\le \frac{25(T-m)}{36H_1}$, and assume the constant $v$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:concentration_ineq} can be chosen uniformly over all models $i\in[m]$ and all pull counts $K\le T$. Then \[ \mathbb P(\hat i_T=i^*) \ge 1-\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{K=1}^T 2\exp(...) \]

results.notes: Stated as P(correct) >= 1 - sum; recorded as an upper bound on error probability. Paper's m (models) mapped to K; the paper's K (pull count) renamed k_pull. Summand independent of i so the sum over i gives factor K. H_1 = sum_i Delta_i^{-2} including Delta_{i*} = min gap. Restated as Theorem 4 in the appendix. Environment marked stochastic_iid only approximately: sampling is without replacement from a finite population.
